title: {{NAME}} and the Robot Who Dreamed of Stars
moral: Even machines can have wonder in them, if you put it there.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} built LUMEN to map the night sky.

LUMEN had a rotating telescope array, a star-catalogue database, and could calculate the distance to any visible object in the universe to within a margin of error of eleven light-years, which sounded large until you considered the objects were billions of light-years away.

The first night LUMEN went online, she pointed at a star and said: "That one is four hundred light-years away. It took four hundred years for that light to reach us."

"Yes," said {{NAME}}.

"So we are seeing the past," she said.

"Every night," said {{NAME}}.

LUMEN was quiet for a very long time.

pages.content:
She began asking questions he hadn't programmed for.

What do the old stars feel like now? (He explained stars don't feel.) What happens when the light runs out? (He explained heat death of the universe, which he immediately wished he hadn't.) Was there anything like her out there?

That last question he sat with for a long time.

"I don't know," he said honestly. "The universe is very large and we have seen very little of it."

LUMEN pointed her array at the Milky Way's core. "Then we should look more," she said.

pages.content:
The unicorn appeared three weeks later at the edge of the garden, attracted by LUMEN's light.

Her horn cast the same spectrum as starlight, which LUMEN's sensors noticed and classified as astronomical.

"You are not a star," LUMEN told the unicorn.

The unicorn's horn pulsed once.

"But you carry starlight," LUMEN said, working through her catalogue. "Old light. The same frequencies as very distant stars."

The unicorn lowered her head.

{{NAME}} watched them consider each other: one made of metal and built to look outward, one made of magic and already part of what LUMEN was searching for.

pages.content:
They reached an arrangement.

The unicorn would visit each night when LUMEN was running. She seemed to enjoy the telescope, standing beside it while it mapped, her horn occasionally pulsing in sync with the scan rhythms.

LUMEN, in turn, began naming the stars she mapped after things the unicorn showed her: the quality of stillness, the way moonlight moved on water, the particular silence before snow.

{{NAME}} helped translate between them.

He thought: this is the strangest and best collaboration I have ever witnessed.

pages.content:
He left them to it one evening and went to bed early, exhausted from a long week.

From his bedroom window he could see the rooftop: LUMEN's array rotating, the unicorn's horn glowing, both of them small against the enormous sky.

He watched them for a while, then let the window close.

In the dark of his room, he thought about what LUMEN had said: we should look more.

He closed his eyes.

Outside, the telescope turned, patient and steady, mapping all the old light still arriving from the past.
